analysis.one_liner: Lets early retirees keep buying their employer's group health insurance until Medicare begins.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote after being referred to three House committees in August 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have extended COBRA continuation coverage — the federal rule that lets workers keep buying their employer's group health plan after a job loss — to retirees. If an employer cut back or ended a retiree health plan, the retiree, spouse, dependent children, or surviving spouse could keep buying the group coverage until they became eligible for Medicare at 65. It was referred to three House committees in August 1995 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Early retirees and their families who counted on employer-paid retiree health coverage and then saw it reduced or eliminated before they qualified for Medicare — a gap where people are too young for Medicare but have lost the employer plan they retired with. They would have gained the right to buy back into the group plan instead of facing the individual insurance market alone.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Early retirees who lost employer health coverage

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new COBRA qualifying event: when an employer substantially reduces or eliminates a retiree group health plan, affected retirees and their dependents gain the right to continuation coverage.
Coverage would run until the retiree becomes entitled to Medicare, closing the gap for people who retire before 65 and then lose their retiree plan.
Protects spouses, dependent children, and surviving spouses as qualified beneficiaries, not just the retiree.

Amends the three core laws governing this coverage — the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code — so the new right applies consistently across the public, private, and tax sides of the law.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor retiree health plans would bear new obligations: they could no longer quietly cut or end retiree coverage without offering continuation coverage, and they would handle the notices and administration. Retirees themselves would pay the premiums out of pocket, as COBRA continuation coverage is purchased by the beneficiary.

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no subsidy. Under COBRA, the person buying continuation coverage typically pays the full premium plus a small administrative fee, which for someone on an early-retirement, pre-Medicare income can be hard to afford — the right to buy coverage is not the same as coverage people can use.
Employers would face a new obligation whenever they trim or end retiree benefits, which could make some employers more hesitant to promise retiree health coverage in the first place.
The trigger is narrow: it covers only a substantial reduction or elimination of a retiree plan, so retirees who lose coverage in other ways would not be helped.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a narrow, targeted fix for a real gap: people who retire before 65 and then lose the retiree health plan they were counting on. The honest costs are that retirees pay full freight for the coverage, and employers take on a new requirement. It would not have fixed retiree health security broadly, but for the specific group it covered, the protection was real and the price mostly fell on employers and the retirees choosing to buy in.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees in August 1995, farmed out to their health subcommittees within two weeks, and then sat untouched until the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Johnson of South Dakota introduced the bill on August 2, 1995, and it was referred to the Committees on Commerce, Ways and Means, and Economic and Educational Opportunities.
Within a matter of days in mid-August 1995, each committee passed it down to a health-related subcommittee — Health, Health and Environment, and Employer-Employee Relations.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the bill's last recorded action is that August 1995 subcommittee referral, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that reduce or eliminate retiree health coverage kept full freedom to do so, with no new continuation obligation. Insurers gained nothing but lost nothing. Retirees who lose employer coverage before Medicare got no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers free to cut retiree health plans

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split is unknown; sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny — one Democrat and one Republican out of 435 House members.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to offer continuation coverage whenever they substantially cut or ended retiree health benefits, limiting their ability to shed that liability. Nothing passed, so they kept that flexibility.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: Retirees buying back into group coverage would have brought premium revenue to plans and insurers. Because retirees pay the full premium themselves, the gain comes alongside the protection retirees wanted.
